 Amazon opened its early Black Friday pricing on portable power stations this week, and the cuts run from a 128Wh box that fits in one hand to a 2,080Wh unit built to sit behind the refrigerator. Every discount in this set lands between 34% and 47% off the listing’s regular price, with no coupon or code standing between the reader and the number. Every station here runs a lithium iron phosphate battery, the chemistry that holds up under daily cycling instead of fading after a couple of seasons. Bluetti holds eight of the eleven slots, because that’s where the deep cuts landed this week.
 The list runs in capacity order, smallest first, with the DJI and Anker entries placed where their watt-hours put them. That keeps the price per watt-hour visible as the boxes grow, and the spread runs from 37 cents to just over a dollar. Read the output figure before the capacity figure on every pick, since a big battery behind a small inverter won’t start a kettle.

 1 BLUETTI Elite 10 Mini
 The Elite 10 Mini is the smallest real power station in this set, and it gives up almost nothing a desk or a carry-on bag actually asks for. A 200W AC outlet on a 128Wh battery covers a laptop, a camera charger and a drone case on a workday or a travel day, without pretending it belongs under a refrigerator.
 The listing puts that 200W AC outlet beside a 100W USB-C port and DC outputs on a 4.0-pound box measuring 7.8 by 5.7 by 4.3 inches. The LiFePO4 pack is rated past 3,000 cycles, and a 10-millisecond UPS switchover guards the gear sitting on your desk. A built-in light with three modes rides on top, so the box handles the tent and the nightstand too. At 128Wh it falls inside the 100 to 160Wh band airlines allow in the cabin with prior approval, capped at two per passenger.
 It’s a power bank with a wall outlet attached.
 BLUETTI Elite 10 Mini 
128Wh LiFePO4 · 200W AC outlet · 100W USB-C port · 4.0 lbs · 3 lighting modes
Price: $119.00 $199.00 (save $80.00, 40% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 2 BLUETTI Elite 30 Mini
 Bluetti built the Elite 30 Mini around one small idea, trivial until you’ve packed a bag in the dark: a retractable USB-C cable built into the case. It pulls out to charge, then disappears when the job’s done, so the most-forgotten item in portable power stops being a packing step.
 Under the trick sits a 288Wh LiFePO4 battery rated past 6,000 cycles, two AC outlets, two 140W bidirectional USB-C ports, a 30W USB-C port, a USB-A port and a 12V car outlet. The whole layout rides on a 7.3-pound frame, with an outage switchover under 10 milliseconds so a router never notices the grid dropping. Three lighting modes remember your last brightness setting, finishing the grab-and-go case for the hallway closet.
 The built-in cable sells this one.
 BLUETTI Elite 30 Mini 
288Wh · 300W · retractable USB-C cable
Price: $239.98 $449.00 (save $209.02, 47% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 3 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2
 Same 288Wh capacity as the Mini above, spent differently. The Elite 30 V2 doubles continuous output to 600W and adds a lifting mode rated at 1,500W, moving a small kettle, a toaster or a CPAP machine from the maybe pile into the covered pile.
 Nine output ports spread across the front of a 9.5-pound box measuring 9.8 by 7 by 6.6 inches. The UPS switchover matches the Mini at 10 milliseconds when the power drops mid-storm and the lights go with it. Bluetti’s UltraCell build keeps standby draw low at 4.5W on DC, so a charged unit in a closet isn’t quietly emptying itself between uses. The fifty dollars over the Mini buys output headroom and nothing else, the right trade when your loads include a heating element.
 Buy this over the Mini for heating loads.
 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 
288Wh LiFePO4 · 600W output, 1,500W lifting · 9 ports · 9.5 lbs
Price: $289.99 $449.00 (save $159.01, 35% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 4 DJI Power 1000 V2
 DJI’s entry is the output bully of the 1kWh class here, rated at 2,600W continuous from a 1,024Wh LFP battery where most rivals stop at 1,800W or less. That headroom covers kettles, power tools and a microwave without tripping the inverter, and at $399.98 it undercuts every other 1kWh station in the roundup.
 Two 140W USB-C ports anchor the front panel, and the case runs as low as 26 decibels in quiet operation. The UPS switchover fires in 10 milliseconds when the grid drops under a desk setup. The catch is printed on the listing itself: the MPPT and car charging modules aren’t built in, so solar or vehicle charging takes a separate DJI adapter that isn’t in the box. Anyone planning a solar-first setup should price that adapter in before calling this the cheap option.
 The strongest 1kWh output here, priced lowest.
 DJI Power 1000 V2 
1,024Wh LFP · 2,600W output
Price: $399.98 $699.00 (save $299.02, 43% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 5 BLUETTI Elite 100 Mini
 The Elite 100 Mini stands its kilowatt-hour upright. The tower footprint measures 9.2 by 8.4 inches at the base, so a full 1,004.8Wh of capacity takes less counter, shelf or truck-bed corner than the flat boxes it competes with. It still weighs a manageable 23.5 pounds by the top handle.
 Output is the compromise here, 700W across three AC outlets with a 1,400W surge ceiling, backed by a 140W USB-C port and DC outputs. The UltraCell LiFePO4 pack carries a 6,000-plus cycle rating, the UPS switchover runs at 10 milliseconds, and a built-in light with three modes can light the counter it’s standing on. Shoppers who need a kettle or a microwave running should walk one slot down to the Elite 100 V2 and take its 1,800W instead.
 A kilowatt-hour that fits a bookshelf corner.
 BLUETTI Elite 100 Mini 
1,004.8Wh · 700W AC, 1,400W surge · 23.5 lbs, tower design
Price: $428.99 $799.00 (save $370.01, 46% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 6 BLUETTI Elite 100 V2
 This is the balanced one in the Bluetti stack, the station in this page’s hero shot, working by the water. A 1,024Wh battery and 1,800W of continuous output with 2,700W of lifting headroom cover the standard camp and outage load list, from the coffee maker to the laptop desk.
 Eleven ports handle the rest of the kit at once, and the LiFePO4 pack is rated past 4,000 cycles. The whole unit weighs 25 pounds in a 12.6 by 8.5 by 9.8 inch case with a hidden handle for one-handed carries. App control over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth covers charging modes, monitoring and firmware from the couch. The UPS switchover holds at 10 milliseconds for the home-office gear it’ll spend most outages protecting. Against the DJI two slots up, it trades raw output for a fuller port spread and built-in charging flexibility.
 The middle of the ladder, done right.
 BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 
1,024Wh LiFePO4 · 1,800W output · 11 ports · 25 lbs
Price: $498.99 $899.00 (save $400.01, 44% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 7 Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2
 Anker’s second-generation C1000 pitches its 1,024Wh at the home desk first and the campsite second, and the feature list reads that way from the top. Output peaks higher than the Elite 100 V2 at 2,000W continuous and 3,000W peak across ten ports, giving it the edge when a blender, a kettle and a monitor land on the same strip.
 The app layer is where Anker separates itself here, with a time-of-use mode that schedules charging around peak rates. A 10-millisecond UPS switchover guards the desk while it does so, keeping a dropped grid out of your work. Solar input accepts up to 600W off-grid, the LiFePO4 pack holds at least 80% of its capacity after 4,000 cycles, and the case measures 15.1 by 8.2 by 9.6 inches. The live price also moved in the buyer’s favor, dropping twenty dollars under where this deal first surfaced.
 The desk-first pick of the 1kWh class.
 Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 
1,024Wh · 2,000W output, 3,000W peak · 10 ports · app time-of-use mode
Price: $529.99 $799.00 (save $269.01, 34% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 8 DJI Power 2000
 Step up to two kilowatt-hours and the math in this roundup turns in the buyer’s favor as the output figure climbs with the capacity it carries. The DJI Power 2000 carries 2,048Wh of LFP capacity and a 3,000W output rating, the highest continuous figure in this list, at a price that works out near 37 cents per watt-hour.
 Fifteen ports include dual SDC sockets for DJI’s own fast-charge gear, and the case runs as low as 30 decibels. The UPS switchover matches the smaller DJI at 10 milliseconds for home backup duty. Capacity expands with DJI’s 2,048Wh expansion batteries when the base unit stops being enough, though those batteries sell separately. The footprint is a fixed 17.64 by 8.86 by 12.76 inches wherever it lands. The smaller DJI’s adapter caveat applies here in full: MPPT and car charging modules aren’t built in, so solar and vehicle charging need separate DJI adapters.
 Cheapest capacity in the set, full stop.
 DJI Power 2000 
2,048Wh LFP · 3,000W output · 15 ports incl. dual SDC
Price: $749.99 $1,299.00 (save $549.01, 42% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 9 BLUETTI Elite 200 V2
 Bluetti’s big box answers the DJI directly, with 2,080Wh of capacity and 2,600W of continuous output that lifts to 3,900W for loads that surge at startup. It’s the home-backup pick for shoppers who want the charging hardware built in rather than adapted on, since it takes wall, solar and vehicle power through the case.
 The automotive-grade LiFePO4 pack is rated past 6,000 cycles, and standby draw sits at 10W so more of the charge survives to the loads. It can run nine devices at once across its outlet spread, from the fridge circuit to the phone chargers. UPS switchover runs at 15 milliseconds on this model, a step behind the 10-millisecond figure on the smaller Elites, so sensitive desktop setups should note the difference. For fridge, freezer and workshop duty, that gap never enters the conversation.
 Built-in everything, at the big-box price.
 BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 
2,080Wh · 2,600W output, 3,900W lifting · 6,000+ cycles
Price: $898.99 $1,399.00 (save $500.01, 36% off)

 10 BLUETTI FridgePower
 One product in this roundup exists for exactly one job, and it’s shaped like it. The FridgePower packs 2,016Wh and 1,800W of output into a slab just 75 millimeters thin, so it slides into the gap behind the refrigerator or mounts on the kitchen wall.
 Standby draw is the spec that sells a fridge battery, and this one sips 4W at idle where conventional stations burn several times that staying awake. The UPS switchover fires in 10 milliseconds when the grid drops, and the app pushes storm alerts ahead of bad weather. Capacity grows to 8,064Wh as BlueCell 200 expansion batteries stack on, for households that lose power for days at a stretch. A separate glance display comes in the box, so the charge state reads from across the kitchen.
 The fridge gets its own battery now.
 BLUETTI FridgePower 
2,016Wh · 1,800W output · 75mm slim, wall-mount ready
Price: $999.00 $1,599.00 (save $600.00, 38% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 11 BLUETTI Charger 1 Alternator Charger (Accessory Pick)
 This one isn’t a power station, and it’s in the roundup because it fixes the weakest link in every station above it. The Charger 1 pulls up to 560W from a vehicle’s alternator while you drive and feeds it to the station in the cargo area. The drive to the trailhead or the cabin stops being dead time for the battery.
 Bluetti rates it for every model in its own line and, by the listing’s count, 95% of third-party power stations, with output adjustable up to 56V. An onboard algorithm watches the vehicle’s starter battery and backs off before the charging load can strand you. An active cooling fan keeps the unit stable in a hot cargo area, and the box includes the 6AWG input cable and installation hardware. It needs a station to feed, which is why it closes the list instead of leading it.
 The road-trip accessory that pays rent.
 BLUETTI Charger 1 
560W alternator charger · 12V/24V input
Price: $218.98 $399.00 (save $180.02, 45% off)

 How to choose your size
 Match the output figure to the single biggest load first, because a station that can’t start your kettle or your microwave is the wrong station at any capacity. Small boxes under 300W of output belong to phones, laptops, cameras and lights, while the 600W to 2,000W middle covers kitchen and workshop loads one at a time. The 2,600W class and up stops asking which appliance is plugged in.
 Capacity gets cheaper as the boxes get bigger, with the DJI Power 2000 landing near $0.37 per watt-hour while the Elite 30 V2 costs $1.01 for every watt-hour it carries. You’re paying for portability at the small end and getting raw storage at a discount at the big end. Buy the DJI Power 1000 V2 at $399.98 if one box has to split camp and outage duty, and skip the small end entirely if a refrigerator or a heating element is on your list.

 Black Friday falls on 27 November, 2026—the perfect time to look for a portable power station for outage backup or off-grid camping. With tons of options available, which power station is worth buying? This guide helps you find the right power setup without paying for features you won’t use.  
 What to Consider When Choosing a Portable Power Station 
 Instead of getting distracted by nice-to-have features like ambient light bars, focus on three core aspects:
 -Capacity (Wh):  Measures stored energy. Higher capacity means longer runtime but adds weight and cost. Calculate your devices’ total power draw and target uptime, factoring in conversion loss.
 -Output power (W):  Determines which appliances you can run. Check continuous rated output and starting (surge) requirements for motor-based devices like fridges.
 -Charging and expansion:  Consider whether you’ll recharge from a wall outlet, solar panels, or your vehicle. If you expect higher needs later, select a power system that supports additional batteries or charging accessories.
 Find the Right Power Station for Your Lifestyle 
 The best portable power station isn’t necessarily perfect; it should solve your everyday power problems. Start by asking what you need to keep running, and for how long. Here’s how you can choose for three common situations.
 Portable Power Station for Daily Backup & Light Outdoor 
 When grid power goes out mid-workday, you mainly need a laptop, Wi-Fi router, and a few lights, about 100–300 W, so a few hours uses under 1 kWh. What matters more is a seamless switchover that keeps your laptop powered mid-meeting. The  BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 ’s UPS mode takes over in under 10 ms. Its 1,024 Wh capacity and 1,800 W output leave room for a small fridge. At around 11.5 kg, it’s also easy to carry outdoors, and a  PV200 solar panel  recharges it when a mains outlet is unavailable.
 Portable Power Station for RVs & Camping 
 On a coastal road trip, you’ll run a 12 V fridge, lights, a water pump, and maybe a water heater. That’s roughly 1–2 kWh a day, or around 3 kWh for a comfortable weekend trip. If you stay longer, flexible charging really matters. The  BLUETTI Elite 300  packs 3 kWh of energy in a compact package and includes a 12 V/30 A DC port for all your camping essentials. Recharge it with a  PV350  or  PV500  solar panel, or add the  Charger 2  for up to 13 times faster charging on the drive.
 High-Power & Off-Grid Solution 
 Full-time vanlife or a rural project is a different story. Saws, grinders, and pumps can pull 1,500–3,000 W and surge higher at startup. The  BLUETTI Apex 300  delivers 3,840 W, surging to 7,680 W for large tools and agricultural equipment. When your needs grow, expand it from 2.76 kWh to 19 kWh for days off-grid. Add a  SORA 500 solar panel for on-site power, or integrate it into a campervan with the  Charger 2 and DC Hub .

 The smartest purchase is not necessarily the biggest battery or the largest advertised discount. It is the power station that delivers the right balance of stored energy, output power, portability, and price for the way you live.
 How to Find the Best Value in a Portable Power Station
 A great deal should give you more than a lower purchase price. It should provide the capacity, performance, and flexibility you will actually use.
 Compare Cost per Watt-Hour
 Cost per watt-hour is a simple way to compare battery capacity against price.
 Cost per Wh = Purchase price ÷ Nominal battery capacity (Wh) 
 For example, a power station priced at $1,000 with a nominal capacity of 2,000Wh has a nominal cost of $0.50 per Wh. This is an illustrative example, not a current BLUETTI offer.
 Use this metric alongside other features:
 table]:w-full!"> 
 Buying factor 
 Why it matters 
 Battery capacity (Wh)
 Determines how much energy is stored for later use
 Continuous output (W)
 Determines which appliances the unit can run at the same time
 Startup / surge capability
 Helps determine whether the unit can start appliances with brief inrush demands, such as compatible motors and compressors
 Power Lifting mode
 Supports specified compatible resistive heating appliances; it is not a substitute for motor or compressor startup capability
 Charging speed
 Helps you replenish energy between uses

 How this tracker works 
 Every morning since Oct 27 we read the EcoFlow, Jackery, BLUETTI and Anker SOLIX US stores and save each station's price. "Lowest we have seen" is the lowest of those mornings, and the small line shows the last 30 days. The crossed-out price, where there is one, is the store's own.
 Every price here is the brand's own US store price. We do not track Amazon prices: an Amazon button opens that exact model on Amazon, where the price can differ.
 Quick answers
 When is BLUETTI Black Friday 2026? Black Friday is Friday, November 27, 2026, and Cyber Monday is November 30. BLUETTI sets its own sale dates; this page shows a new price the morning after the store changes it.
 How do I know a Black Friday price is really low? Compare it with the lowest price we have seen. The BLUETTI store sold the Elite 400 for $1,399 on Oct 27 and charges $1,499 today, so a Black Friday price above $1,399 is not its lowest price this fall.
 Are these prices for the station alone? Yes. Bundles with solar panels are left out, and where a station comes in more than one color, the price is the cheapest color in stock.
 Can I get an email when a price drops? Yes. Every station page has a price alert: leave your email and the price you want, and we email you once when the store price reaches it.
